analysis.one_liner: Cuts the standard workweek from 40 to 32 hours and requires overtime after eight hours a day.
analysis.headline: The bill went no further than a committee referral and never received a hearing or a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, the law behind the 40-hour week and overtime rules, to lower the standard workweek to 32 hours over three years [S2][S3]. Hours worked beyond 32 in a week would earn 1.5 times regular pay, hours beyond 8 in a day 1.5 times pay, and hours beyond 12 in a day double pay [S3]. The change phases in through 38, 36, and 34 hours before reaching 32 [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers covered by federal overtime law, who would either work fewer hours for the same weekly pay or earn premium pay for hours beyond 32, plus workers who regularly put in long days and would earn more for hours past 8 or 12 in a day [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly workers covered by overtime law

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the overtime threshold from 40 hours a week to 32 hours over a three-year phase-in, so hours worked past 32 would be paid at 1.5 times the regular rate [S2][S3].
Adds a daily overtime trigger that federal law does not have today: 1.5 times pay for workdays over 8 hours and double pay for workdays over 12 hours [S3].
Phases the change in through 38, 36, and 34 hours before reaching 32, giving employers a step-down period [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with hourly staff, who would pay premium rates for hours now treated as regular time, and potentially customers through higher prices; workers could also face reduced schedules or slower weekly pay if employers adjust instead of paying premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise labor costs for any employer whose staff works more than 32 hours a week, and it does not include a revenue offset or small-business exception in the text provided [S3].

Because the Fair Labor Standards Act requires overtime pay but does not set weekly pay, employers can legally respond by cutting hours or base rates, which could leave some workers with the same or lower weekly pay while working fewer hours [S3].
Mandating overtime after 8 hours a day can push employers toward unpredictable part-time scheduling rather than stable full-time shifts, a known effect of strict daily overtime rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who regularly work long weeks, the bill promises either more free time at the same pay or higher premium pay — a substantial, broad benefit. The cost falls on employers as higher overtime bills, and the risk is that some respond by cutting hours, schedules, or pay growth rather than absorbing it. A three-year phase-in softens the shock but does not guarantee workers keep their weekly income. It was an ambitious, untested shift in the national standard, and it never got a hearing where these tradeoffs could be debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano (D-CA) introduced the bill on July 27, 2021, with three original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the same day, and no further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S5].
It finished the Congress with 17 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that would have paid overtime after 32 hours a week and 8 hours a day are better off, since the standard stayed at 40 hours a week with no daily trigger.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers; the workweek standard stayed at 40

for.name: Rep. Mark Takano
for.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Subcommittee on Workforce Protections; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push in the committee with jurisdiction over wage and hour law.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction under Rep. Bobby Scott (D-VA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing or markup in the 16 months the bill was pending, so it never reached the floor.

against.name: Employer and business lobby groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed shortening the standard workweek, arguing it would sharply raise labor costs for businesses that rely on more-than-32-hour schedules.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on [S4]; no vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call to measure the split.

industries.industry: Employers of hourly workers (retail, food service, healthcare staffing, manufacturing)
industries.note: The bill would make hours now counted as regular time eligible for 1.5-times pay after 32 hours a week, and after 8 and 12 hours a day, directly raising payroll costs [S3]. Employers' interest in keeping the 40-hour standard ran against workers' interest in shorter weeks and premium pay [S2][S3].
Workers exempt from federal overtime rules today would gain if the shortened week brought them coverage, though the bill text provided does not change exemption classifications [S3].
